topic.title: The clubhouse sells the flat, not you
topic.claim: The swimming pool in the brochure was built to sell the flat at a higher rate, not for you to swim in.
topic.moment: You pay maintenance every month for a pool, a gym and a mini theatre, and you've used the lift.

turn.believed: Amenities add to your life in the society.
turn.actually: Amenities add to the price per square foot, and you pay for them in maintenance forever.

topic.feeling: Like I'm paying rent on a lifestyle I never lived.
topic.villain: Builders who price flats on amenity lists.
topic.because: A long amenity list lets the builder charge more for the same flat. Once the flats are sold, the running cost is passed to residents.
topic.payoff: Before you buy, ask what the maintenance will be in five years, and which amenities you'll use more than once a month.
topic.behaviour: Builders advertise pools, clubhouses and jogging tracks; residents pay high maintenance for facilities few use.
topic.mechanism: Amenities raise the sale price, then running costs pass to buyers.
topic.group: First-time flat buyers in their late 20s and early 30s
topic.send_to: The couple currently visiting sample flats every weekend.
topic.why_now: Flat prices keep rising, and amenities are part of how builders justify the jump.

score.why: You pay maintenance on a pool you've never used. Amenities set the price per square foot.

paragraphs: The society pool was never built for you. It was built to sell your flat.
Swipe to read →
Every new tower in India sells the same dream. Pool, gym, clubhouse, jogging track, mini theatre.
Oh, and a flat somewhere in there.
Our parents bought a flat for its walls and its water supply. We buy one for the clubhouse photo in the brochure.
Here's the trick. A longer amenity list means a higher price per square foot.
For the same two bedrooms.
Then the builder hands the society over and leaves. The pool stays. So does the bill.
It's called maintenance.

This is why:
– the pool is shut half the year
– the gym has one working treadmill
– the theatre opens for birthdays
I get why we fall for it. In a brochure, a pool looks like the life we moved to the city for.
**The builder sold you the pool once. You pay for it every month.**

violations: Slide 4: "A ₹3,000 monthly maintenance bill is ₹36,000 a year. That covers a pool you went into once, the first summer." Maintenance pays for the lift, guard, parking, power and common areas, not just the pool. Presenting the whole bill as the cost of the pool is a basic error about who pays for what (hard failure 12). "Went into once, the first summer" is also an invented scene detail that contradicts slide 3's "You saw them on Diwali".

Slide 9: "Ask what the maintenance will be in five years... If the honest answer is the lift, that's all you should be paying extra for." This is a how-to instruction and a tidy moral, with no line to repeat and no sting (hard failure 8). It also leaves the reader on advice rather than the feeling.

Slide 7: The Noida tenant ₹700 pool fee and the RWA justification read as a news recap and drift off the point. The pool fee falls on tenants and is a separate issue from the builder's pricing trick. The slide adds nothing the reader doesn't already have by slide 6, and its closing line ("a cost that someone has to pay") restates slides 4 to 6, so it is a dead slide (hard failure 7).
Slides 3 and 4 both say "you don't use the pool and still pay." Slide 4 is a dead slide because it repeats slide 3's point, and the repeat is shaky because the details contradict each other.
notes: Slide 4: Delete it, or rebuild it around the real number. The sourced ₹3,000 is a whole-society maintenance figure, so show the amenity part as a share of that bill, without claiming the whole ₹36,000 pays for the pool. Better still, merge it into slide 3 so the idea is said once and the post gets shorter.

Slide 9: Replace the instruction with a stinging closer in his voice. Keep the five-year maintenance and used-more-than-once-a-month test only as a quiet observation, not a command. For example, end on the builder selling the pool once and the resident paying for it every month. Cut "you should" and "skip the clubhouse tour".

sources.fact: ThePrint reports that pools, gyms and clubhouses were marketed as lifestyle benefits but now cause friction over charges. Tenants in Noida societies pay fixed maintenance plus extra pool fees, and pool use is restricted. The article does not show that pools were built only to raise prices.
sources.excerpt: the fixed Rs 3,000 maintenance charges | The maintenance charges are used to maintain the equipment and facilities that residents use. | Charges for Tenants: ₹700 per person for the season! | the dream of gated-community living | often marketed as key lifestyle benefits

sources.fact: Noida RWAs charge tenants extra amenity fees for the pool and gym on top of maintenance. They say the fees cover running costs and control access, so the pool carries a recurring cost for residents.
sources.excerpt: these charges have been implemented to regulate access, maintain society and cover the cost of running shared facilities. | tenants are charged Rs 500 for 'amenity charge' for an individual and Rs 1,000 for a family. | tenants and owners are both charged for the pool and the gym. | there are no rules regarding ownership and charges for tenants.

slides.why_swipe: Built to sell? Then what is my maintenance paying for?

paragraphs: We call it maintenance, as if it's for a leaking pipe and a lobby repaint.
It also keeps the pool, the gym and the theatre running, whether you walk in or not.
slides.why_swipe: So what do you actually use?

paragraphs:
Three years in, here is what you actually use:
- the lift, twice a day
- your parking slot
- the guard who calls before Swiggy comes up
slides.why_swipe: And the stuff on the brochure?

paragraphs: The pool, the gym with the mirror wall and the mini theatre? You saw them on Diwali.
Walk past the clubhouse on a weekday evening. An empty deck and the sharp smell of chlorine. The theatre unlocks when someone's kid turns six.
slides.why_swipe: So why does every tower still sell this?

paragraphs: From the selling side, the logic is plain. A long amenity list lets the price per square foot go up for the same two bedrooms.
Then the builder hands over the society. The chlorine, the lifeguard and the broken treadmill move onto your maintenance bill.
slides.why_swipe: So what did the pool actually cost you?

paragraphs: You paid for the pool twice.
Once in the price. Then every month.
slides.why_swipe: So why do smart buyers keep signing up?

paragraphs: It isn't foolishness. After years of PG rooms and landlords with rules, a pool outside your window feels like proof that you made it.
That feeling is exactly what the brochure is selling.
slides.why_swipe: So how do you see through it?

paragraphs: Here's a test for your next sample flat visit. Count the amenities you'd honestly use more than once a month.
Then watch the sales executive point at the pool again.

draft.caption: The costliest subscription most of us have is a pool we only see from the balcony.
draft.alt_text: An eight-slide text post arguing that the pool in a builder's brochure exists to sell the flat, not for residents to swim in. Monthly maintenance keeps the pool, gym and theatre running whether residents use them or not, while most people only use the lift, parking and security. It describes an empty clubhouse on a weekday evening and a theatre that opens for kids' birthdays. It explains that a long amenity list lets the price per square foot rise for the same flat, and after handover the running costs move onto the residents' maintenance bill, so buyers pay for the pool twice: once in the price, then every month. It says buyers fall for it after years of PG rooms because a pool feels like proof of making it, and ends with a test: count the amenities you'd use more than once a month, then watch the sales executive point at the pool again.

claims.text: Maintenance charges are used to maintain the equipment and facilities residents use, including the pool and gym
